messages.text: To get started, could you tell me what you enjoy most about your work?
TEST I write software. I enjoy solving tricky problems.

It’s great that you enjoy solving tricky problems in your software work. When you think about your day-to-day tasks, is there anything else you particularly enjoy—for example, collaborating with others, learning new technologies, or seeing your code used by real people—or is the problem-solving aspect mainly what makes the work satisfying for you?
TEST Meetings. Far too many meetings.

Thanks for clarifying. It sounds like the problem‑solving side of writing software is what you enjoy, and the many meetings are more of a drawback than a positive.

Looking at the other side of things: what would you say is the hardest or most challenging part of your work?

That makes sense — having your concentration broken by frequent meetings can make deep work really difficult.

Aside from meetings interrupting your focus, is there anything else you find particularly hard or challenging about your work, such as deadlines, unclear requirements, technical complexity, or teamwork issues? Or are the interruptions to your concentration really the main challenge for you?

Thanks, I understand — we can leave it at that.

That was actually the last topic I needed to cover, so we’re all done with the interview. Thank you for taking the time to answer these questions.

messages.text: Thanks for taking the time to chat. To start us off: when you need to learn something new for your job, what’s the very first thing you usually do?
TEST Mostly by trying things out and asking colleagues.
Got it—so you like to dive in and experiment, then talk to colleagues. Can you walk me through a recent example of something new you had to figure out at work, and how you went about it step by step?
TEST Sometimes short online courses, but rarely.

Nice, that’s helpful. Let’s stick with a concrete example: can you think of a specific thing you recently had to learn for work (like a new tool, process, or type of task), and describe what you actually did first, then what you tried next, and how colleagues or any online course fit into it?
Thank you for your answers — this concludes the interview.
